claims.claim: More than half of the entire adult human population is latently infected with human cytomegalovirus (HCMV).
claims.source: More than half of the entire adult human population and over 90% of the elderly in developing countries are latently infected with the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV, human betaherpesvirus 5 [HHV-5]; NCBI taxonomy ID 10359) (Fowler et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2022

claims.claim: Over 90% of the elderly in developing countries are latently infected with HCMV.
claims.source: More than half of the entire adult human population and over 90% of the elderly in developing countries are latently infected with the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV, human betaherpesvirus 5 [HHV-5]; NCBI taxonomy ID 10359) (Fowler et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2022

claims.claim: More than half of all immune parameters are altered in HCMV-infected individuals.
claims.source: Accordingly, more than half of all immune parameters are altered in HCMV-infected individuals (Brodin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Brodin et al., 2015

claims.claim: The depletion of CD4+ cells together with IFNγ results in CMV reactivation in more than 75% of animals.
claims.source: Accordingly, the depletion of CD4 + cells together with IFNγ results in CMV reactivation in more than 75% of animals (Polić et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Polić et al., 1998

claims.claim: The absence of IFN-induced signaling renders mice extremely vulnerable to CMV infections.
claims.source: In accordance with the relevance of IFNs, the absence of IFN-induced signaling renders mice extremely vulnerable to CMV infections (Gil et al., 2001; Le Trilling et al., 2018; Strobl et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gil et al., 2001; Le Trilling et al., 2018; Strobl et al., 2005

claims.claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells produce IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B.
claims.source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells were shown to produce IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B (Gamadia et al., 2004)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gamadia et al., 2004

claims.claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells lyse HCMV antigen-expressing cells in vitro.
claims.source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells were shown to produce IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B (Gamadia et al., 2004) and to lyse HCMV antigen-expressing cells in vitro (van Leeuwen et al., 2006; van Leeuwen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to van Leeuwen et al., 2006; van Leeuwen et al., 2004

claims.claim: CD4+ T cell-mediated immunity is crucial for CMV control in mouse models in vivo.
claims.source: Accordingly, CD4 + T cell-mediated immunity is crucial for CMV control in mouse models in vivo (Jonjić et al., 1989; Jonjić et al., 1990; Walton et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Jonjić et al., 1989; Jonjić et al., 1990; Walton et al., 2008

claims.claim: CD4+ T cells are fundamental to prevent HCMV reactivation in immunocompromised patients receiving solid organ allografts.
claims.source: Furthermore, CD4 + T cells are fundamental to prevent HCMV reactivation in immunocompromised patients receiving solid organ allografts (Lim et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2020

claims.claim: Insufficient CD4+ T cell levels in transplant recipients are associated with recurrent HCMV reactivation, end-organ disease, and an increased likelihood of lethal infections.
claims.source: CD4 + T cells are fundamental to prevent HCMV reactivation in immunocompromised patients receiving solid organ allografts (Lim et al., 2020) or hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), while insufficient CD4 + T cell levels in transplant recipients are associated with recurrent HCMV reactivation, end-organ disease, and an increased likelihood of lethal infections (Einsele et al., 1993; Gabanti et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Einsele et al., 1993; Gabanti et al., 2015

claims.claim: CIITA is the essential and sufficient master regulator of the transcription of the genes in the HLA-II locus.
claims.source: Constitutive as well as IFNγ-induced HLA-II expression are both mediated by the class II transactivator (CIITA), which is the essential and sufficient master regulator of the transcription of the genes in the HLA-II locus.
claims.evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about CIITA function

claims.claim: CIITA and its co-factors control the expression of the classical HLA-II molecules DR, DQ, DP, the non-classical HLA-II peptidome editors DM and DO, and the invariant chain (Ii, also known as CD74).
claims.source: Accordingly, CIITA and its co-factors control the expression of the classical HLA-II molecules DR, DQ, DP, the non-classical HLA-II peptidome editors DM and DO, and the invariant chain (Ii, also known as CD74) (Boss and Jensen, 2003; Ting and Trowsdale, 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Boss and Jensen, 2003; Ting and Trowsdale, 2002

claims.claim: The absence of functional CIITA results in a loss of HLA-II presentation, leading to a hereditary immunodeficiency called type II bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS).
claims.source: The absence of functional CIITA results in a loss of HLA-II presentation, leading to a hereditary immunodeficiency called type II bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS) that causes an extreme vulnerability to infections.
claims.evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about BLS

claims.claim: BLS patients frequently suffer from severe, persistent HCMV infections.
claims.source: In accordance with the relevance of CD4 + T cells and CIITA-driven HLA-II presentation, BLS patients frequently suffer from severe, persistent HCMV infections (Elhasid and Etzioni, 1996; Klein et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Elhasid and Etzioni, 1996; Klein et al., 1993

claims.claim: pUS28 is among the few viral proteins abundantly expressed during both productive replication as well as experimental and natural latency.
claims.source: Importantly, pUS28 is among the few viral proteins abundantly expressed during both productive replication as well as experimental and natural latency (Beisser et al., 2001; Cheung et al., 2006; Goodrum et al., 2002; Krishna et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Beisser et al., 2001; Cheung et al., 2006; Goodrum et al., 2002; Krishna et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2017a

claims.claim: IFNγ induced the upregulation of HLA-DP on the surface of HCMV-permissive fibroblasts.
claims.source: IFNγ induced the upregulation of HLA-DP on the surface of HCMV-permissive fibroblasts (Figure 1A and B)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B

claims.claim: IFNα and TNFα treatment did not induce HLA-DP upregulation on fibroblasts.
claims.source: IFNγ induced the upregulation of HLA-DP on the surface of HCMV-permissive fibroblasts (Figure 1A and B), whereas this was not the case after treatment with IFNα or TNFα (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claims.claim: Longer periods of IFNγ incubation led to an increase of HLA-DP and HLA-DR on the cell surface.
claims.source: Longer periods of IFNγ incubation led to an increase of HLA-DP and HLA-DR on the cell surface (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claims.claim: The upregulation of HLA-DP by IFNγ was prevented in HCMV-infected cells.
claims.source: In clear contrast to uninfected fibroblasts, the upregulation of HLA-DP by IFNγ was prevented in HCMV-infected cells (Figure 1D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E

claims.claim: HCMV mutants lacking the US2-6 or the US2-11 gene region showed the same inhibitory phenotype on HLA-DP upregulation as wild-type HCMV.
claims.source: Interestingly, the same inhibitory phenotype was observed upon infection with HCMV mutants lacking the US2-6 or the US2-11 gene region (Figure 1D and E)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E

claims.claim: HCMV encodes so far unknown antagonists of IFNγ-induced HLA-DP presentation located outside of the US2-11 gene region.
claims.source: These data indicate that HCMV encodes so far unknown antagonists of IFNγ-induced HLA-DP presentation located outside of the US2-11 gene region.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing that US2-11 deletion mutants still inhibit HLA-DP

claims.claim: pUS28 was identified as a candidate antagonist of HLA-DP induction in a screen of HCMV genes.
claims.source: The screen provided candidates for the observed antagonism of HLA-DP induction, including pUS9, pUS19, pp65-UL83, and pUS28.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental screening data described in the text and Figure 2A

claims.claim: pUS28 reproducibly diminished CIITA-induced HLA-DP surface expression.
claims.source: Validation experiments substantiated that pUS28 was reproducibly capable of significantly diminishing CIITA-induced HLA-DP surface expression (Figure 2B and data not shown).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claims.claim: pUS28 significantly diminished the cell surface expression of HLA-DR.
claims.source: Similar to its effect on HLA-DP, pUS28 also significantly diminished the cell surface expression of the presenting molecules HLA-DR (Figure 2C and D)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D

claims.claim: pUS28 significantly diminished the cell surface expression of HLA-DQ.
claims.source: Similar to its effect on HLA-DP, pUS28 also significantly diminished the cell surface expression of the presenting molecules HLA-DR (Figure 2C and D) and HLA-DQ (Figure 2D)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claims.claim: pUS28 significantly diminished the cell surface expression of HLA-DM.
claims.source: pUS28 also significantly diminished the cell surface expression of the presenting molecules HLA-DR (Figure 2C and D) and HLA-DQ (Figure 2D) as well as the peptide editor HLA-DM (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claims.claim: pUS28 dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DR at different levels of CIITA abundance.
claims.source: While increasing amounts of CIITA dose-dependently drove HLA-DP and HLA-DR expression in transfected cells, pUS28 significantly and dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DR (Figure 2E)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claims.claim: pUS28 dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DP at different levels of CIITA abundance.
claims.source: While increasing amounts of CIITA dose-dependently drove HLA-DP and HLA-DR expression in transfected cells, pUS28 significantly and dose-dependently inhibited surface levels of HLA-DR (Figure 2E) and HLA-DP (Figure 2F), at different levels of CIITA abundance.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claims.claim: The levels of CIITA mRNA remained unaltered in the presence of pUS28.
claims.source: Irrespective of the presence or absence of pUS28, the levels of tagged as well as untagged CIITA mRNA remained unaltered (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claims.claim: pUS28 co-expression drastically reduced CIITA protein amounts.
claims.source: In contrast to the unchanged mRNA levels of CIITA, a parallel evaluation of CIITA protein amounts revealed a drastic reduction upon pUS28 co-expression (Figure 3B)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claims.claim: pUS28 has a post-transcriptional effect on CIITA.
claims.source: In contrast to the unchanged mRNA levels of CIITA, a parallel evaluation of CIITA protein amounts revealed a drastic reduction upon pUS28 co-expression (Figure 3B), suggesting a post-transcriptional effect of pUS28 on CIITA.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that mRNA levels remain unchanged while protein levels decrease

claims.claim: The CIITA down-modulating capacity of pUS28 is specific for CIITA and does not affect control proteins such as EYFP.
claims.source: The CIITA down-modulating capacity of pUS28 was observed with different plasmid preparations (Figure 3C), and was specific for CIITA, since control proteins such as the enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (EYFP) remained unaffected (Figure 3C)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claims.claim: The effect of pUS28 on CIITA is not a general capacity of viral chemokine receptor homologs, as pUS27 did not decrease CIITA protein amounts.
claims.source: The effect on CIITA was also not an overarching capacity of viral chemokine receptor homologs, since the protein pUS27, a GPCR encoded by the neighboring gene in the viral genome, did not decrease CIITA protein amounts (Figure 3D)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claims.claim: pUS27 did not decrease HLA-DP surface levels.
claims.source: The effect on CIITA was also not an overarching capacity of viral chemokine receptor homologs, since the protein pUS27, a GPCR encoded by the neighboring gene in the viral genome, did not decrease CIITA protein amounts (Figure 3D) or HLA-DP surface levels (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry analyses confirmed the significant downregulation of CIITA by pUS28.
claims.source: These unbiased MS analyses confirmed the significant downregulation of CIITA by pUS28 (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F

claims.claim: pUS28 led to a significant upregulation of IL-6.
claims.source: In agreement with previous data, pUS28 led to a significant upregulation of IL-6 (Slinger et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Slinger et al., 2010

claims.claim: pUS28 attenuated AP-1 components including JunD.
claims.source: In agreement with previous data, pUS28 led to a significant upregulation of IL-6 (Slinger et al., 2010), and attenuated AP-1 components (Krishna et al., 2019) (here JunD) (Figure 4D and E)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E and citation to Krishna et al., 2019

claims.claim: CD74 was significantly induced by CIITA, unless pUS28 was co-expressed.
claims.source: Conversely, CD74 - the invariant chain required for proper maturation and loading of HLA class II molecules - was significantly induced by CIITA, unless pUS28 was co-expressed (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claims.claim: The negative effect of pUS28 on CIITA-driven CD74 expression was confirmed by flow cytometry.
claims.source: The negative effect of pUS28 on CIITA-driven CD74 expression was confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claims.claim: pUS28 elicits the negative effect on CIITA target genes independent of their genomic localization in the MHC-II locus.
claims.source: In contrast to several other CIITA-regulated genes, CD74 is not encoded by the HLA-II locus on chromosome 6. Thus, the fact that pUS28 prevents CIITA-induced CD74 induction suggests that pUS28 elicits the negative effect on CIITA target genes independent of their genomic localization in the MHC-II locus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that pUS28 affects CD74, which is not in the HLA-II locus

claims.claim: HLA-DP cell surface levels were significantly decreased upon pUS28 induction in doxycycline-inducible fibroblasts.
claims.source: While doxycycline treatment in parental and pUS27-expressing fibroblasts had no significant effect on the IFNγ-induced HLA-DP expression, HLA-DP cell surface levels were significantly decreased upon pUS28 induction (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claims.claim: Wild-type HCMV significantly decreased the percentage of HLA-DP- and HLA-DR-positive cells compared to mock-treated cells.
claims.source: In accordance with aforementioned data, wt HCMV significantly decreased the percentage of HLA-DP- and HLA-DR-positive cells in comparison to mock-treated cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and Figure 5B and C

claims.claim: ΔUS28-HCMV showed an impaired ability to downregulate HLA-II compared to wild-type HCMV.
claims.source: In contrast, ΔUS28-HCMV showed an impaired ability to downregulate HLA-II (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C

claims.claim: pM33 and pUS28 both downregulate human and mouse CIITA.
claims.source: We found that pM33 and pUS28 both downregulate human and mouse CIITA, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved function.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E

claims.claim: The ability of pUS28 to decrease HLA class II expression is evolutionarily conserved.
claims.source: We found that pM33 and pUS28 both downregulate human and mouse CIITA, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved function.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that both pUS28 and its MCMV homolog pM33 downregulate CIITA

claims.claim: pUS28 and CIITA physically interact and form complexes.
claims.source: The IP of pUS28 co-purified CIITA (Figure 6A, upper panel) and vice versa (Figure 6A, lower panel), indicating that both proteins form physical complexes.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A

claims.claim: pUS28 reduces the half-life of CIITA.
claims.source: Despite the inherently short half-life of CIITA (Schnappauf et al., 2003), we observed a more rapid CIITA decay when pUS28 was co-expressed (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6B

claims.claim: A panel of inhibitors targeting different cellular degradation pathways failed to significantly and reproducibly restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, a panel of inhibitors targeting different cellular degradation pathways (e.g. the inhibitors of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway MG-132 and Bortezomib, the inhibitors of UBA3-dependent neddylation blocking cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase activity MLN4924 and TAS4464, the autophagy inhibitors bafilomycin and 3-MA, the inhibitors of lysosomal acidification chloroquine and ammonium chloride, the pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK, the protease inhibitors Pepstatin A, E-64, PMSF, and a pan-protease inhibitor cocktail, as well as the dynamin inhibitor Dynasore and the convertase inhibitor Decanoyl-RVKR-CMK) all failed to significantly and reproducibly restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and data not shown)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: pUS28 reduces CIITA levels either by redundant or unusual degradation processes.
claims.source: all failed to significantly and reproducibly restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and data not shown), implying that pUS28 reduces CIITA levels either by redundant or unusual degradation processes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the failure of multiple degradation pathway inhibitors to restore CIITA

claims.claim: R129A-pUS28 is a mutant that harbors a single amino acid substitution at position 129 (arginine to alanine) within the canonical DRY motif, abrogating G-protein signaling without compromising the subcellular localization or internalization.
claims.source: The latter is a well-studied mutant of pUS28 that harbors a single amino acid substitution at position 129 (arginine to alanine) within the canonical DRY motif, abrogating G-protein signaling without compromising the subcellular localization or internalization (Waldhoer et al., 2003; visualized in Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Waldhoer et al., 2003 and visualization in Figure 7A

claims.claim: Both wt-pUS28 and R129A-pUS28 diminished CIITA protein levels.
claims.source: Both pUS28 variants diminished CIITA protein levels (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claims.claim: The intracellular C terminus of pUS28 is indispensable for CIITA degradation.
claims.source: Conversely, the intracellular C terminus turned out to be indispensable for the CIITA degradation (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claims.claim: R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DP.
claims.source: In accordance with these findings, R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DP (Figure 7D)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claims.claim: R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DR.
claims.source: In accordance with these findings, R129A-pUS28 and wt-pUS28 similarly diminished the surface expression of HLA-DP (Figure 7D) and HLA-DR (Figure 7E)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claims.claim: The mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not diminish HLA-DP surface expression.
claims.source: while the mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not (Figure 7F and G)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F

claims.claim: The mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not diminish HLA-DR surface expression.
claims.source: while the mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not (Figure 7F and G)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G

claims.claim: pUS28 targets CIITA through its C terminus.
claims.source: while the mutant lacking the C terminus (US28-ΔC) did not (Figure 7F and G), indicating that pUS28 targets CIITA through its C terminus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that C-terminal deletion abolishes CIITA targeting

claims.claim: pUS28-ΔC co-purified CIITA in immunoprecipitation experiments.
claims.source: In IP experiments, pUS28-ΔC co-purified CIITA (Figure 7H)
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7H

claims.claim: The lack of the C terminus of pUS28 did not impair the physical interaction with CIITA but rather affected the degradation machinery.
claims.source: In IP experiments, pUS28-ΔC co-purified CIITA (Figure 7H), suggesting that the lack of the C terminus of pUS28 did not impair the physical interaction with CIITA but rather affected the degradation machinery.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that pUS28-ΔC still binds CIITA but does not degrade it

claims.claim: Amino acids in proximity to the transmembrane domain 7 of pUS28 were required for downregulation of CIITA.
claims.source: Further investigations of the C-terminal part of pUS28 revealed that amino acids in proximity to the transmembrane domain 7 were required for downregulation of CIITA as only a mutant lacking the whole C terminus completely lost the capability to target CIITA (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I

claims.claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells.
claims.source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells, but not to control cells that did not express CIITA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claims.claim: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells did not respond to control cells that did not express CIITA.
claims.source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells, but not to control cells that did not express CIITA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claims.claim: The response of HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells to CIITA-expressing cells indicates a specific HLA-II-dependent T cell activation.
claims.source: HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells from HCMV-positive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells, but not to control cells that did not express CIITA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating a specific HLA-II-dependent T cell activation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that T cells respond only to CIITA-expressing cells

claims.claim: In the presence of pUS28 or R129A-pUS28, the immune recognition of CIITA-expressing, antigen-loaded cells by HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells was significantly reduced.
claims.source: In the presence of pUS28 or the mutant R129A-pUS28, the immune recognition of CIITA-expressing, antigen-loaded cells by HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells was significantly reduced (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claims.claim: Supernatants from HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells stimulated with CIITA-expressing cells strongly inhibited HCMV-induced EGFP expression.
claims.source: Supernatants from HCMV-specific CD4 + T cells stimulated with CIITA-expressing cells strongly inhibited HCMV-induced EGFP expression
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D

claims.claim: Supernatants derived from CD4+ T cells stimulated in the presence of pUS28 showed diminished antiviral activity.
claims.source: while supernatants derived from CD4 + T cells stimulated in the presence of pUS28 showed diminished antiviral activity (Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D

claims.claim: pUS28 inhibits the CIITA-driven and HLA-II-dependent CD4+ T cell activation in terms of the production of antiviral cytokines.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that pUS28 inhibits the CIITA-driven and HLA-II-dependent CD4 + T cell activation in terms of the production of antiviral cytokines.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that pUS28 reduces T cell activation and antiviral activity of supernatants

claims.claim: pUS28 acts as calcium-mobilizing beta chemokine receptor.
claims.source: Briefly after its discovery as HCMV-encoded GPCR (Chee et al., 1990), the striking homology of pUS28 to human CX3CR1 was noticed (Gao et al., 1993) and its functionality as calcium-mobilizing beta chemokine receptor was documented (Gao and Murphy, 1994).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gao and Murphy, 1994

claims.claim: pUS28 can act as a co-factor for HIV entry.
claims.source: For example, it can act as a co-factor for the HIV entry (Pleskoff et al., 1997)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pleskoff et al., 1997

claims.claim: pUS28 mediates G protein-coupled intracellular signaling.
claims.source: it mediates G protein-coupled intracellular signaling (Billstrom et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Billstrom et al., 1998

claims.claim: pUS28 sequesters RANTES/MCP-1.
claims.source: it sequesters RANTES/MCP-1 (Bodaghi et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bodaghi et al., 1998

claims.claim: pUS28 serves as fractalkine receptor.
claims.source: and serves as fractalkine receptor (Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998

claims.claim: pUS28 mediates vascular smooth muscle cell migration.
claims.source: it mediates vascular smooth muscle cell migration (Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998; Melnychuk et al., 2004; Streblow et al., 1999; Streblow et al., 2003)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Burg et al., 2015; Kledal et al., 1998; Melnychuk et al., 2004; Streblow et al., 1999; Streblow et al., 2003

claims.claim: pUS28 may act as an oncogene or onco-modulatory protein.
claims.source: and it may act as an oncogene or onco-modulatory protein (Bongers et al., 2010; Maussang et al., 2006; Slinger et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bongers et al., 2010; Maussang et al., 2006; Slinger et al., 2010

claims.claim: pUS28 targets MNDA/PYHIN3 and IFI16/PYHIN2 for rapid degradation.
claims.source: Elegant work by the Sinclair laboratory revealed that pUS28, besides its function as GPCR and latency regulator, targets certain host proteins such as MNDA/PYHIN3 and IFI16/PYHIN2 for rapid degradation.
claims.evidence: Draws from work by the Sinclair laboratory as described in the text

claims.claim: The degradation of MNDA/PYHIN3 and IFI16/PYHIN2 by pUS28 was dependent on GPCR signaling.
claims.source: In contrast to the effect on CIITA shown here, however, this degradation was dependent on GPCR signaling as indicated by the restoration of target protein levels when R129 was mutated (Elder et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Elder et al., 2019

claims.claim: Latently infected primary human CD14+ monocytes exhibit less HLA-DR on the surface compared to uninfected cells.
claims.source: Importantly, Elder et al., 2019 and Slobedman et al., 2002 showed that latently infected primary human CD14 + monocytes and human fetal liver hematopoietic cells exhibit less HLA-DR on the surface compared to uninfected cells (Elder et al., 2019; Slobedman et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Elder et al., 2019 and Slobedman et al., 2002

claims.claim: There is an inverse correlation between HCMV transcripts and CD74 as well as HLA-II expression in CD14+ monocytes.
claims.source: which is very well in line with findings by Shnayder et al., 2020 who showed an inverse correlation between HCMV transcripts and CD74 as well as HLA-II expression in CD14 + monocytes (Shnayder et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Shnayder et al., 2020

claims.claim: The deletion of the MCMV US28 homolog M33 results in altered MHC-I presentation in an allotype-specific manner.
claims.source: Recent work with the MCMV model showed that the deletion of the US28 homolog M33 results in altered MHC-I presentation in an allotype-specific manner (H-2Ld and H-2Kd being downregulated in an M33-dependent manner, but not H-2Dd) (White et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2022

claims.claim: HCMV counteracts IFNγ-induced gene expression, partly by inducing the proteasomal degradation of JAK1.
claims.source: Work by Miller et al., 1998 showed that HCMV counteracts IFNγ-induced gene expression, partly by inducing the proteasomal degradation of JAK1, leading to diminished CIITA and HLA-DRα induction when HCMV-infected cells are exposed to IFNγ (Miller et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Miller et al., 1998

claims.claim: HCMV targets constitutive as well as induced CIITA-dependent HLA-II expression at multiple levels by a multipronged attack.
claims.source: Furthermore, HCMV targets constitutive as well as induced CIITA-dependent HLA-II expression at multiple levels by a multipronged attack, comprising the inhibition of (I) IFN-JAK-STAT signaling (Le et al., 2008; Le Trilling et al., 2020; Miller et al., 1998), (II) constitutive CIITA transcription (Lee et al., 2011; Sandhu and Buchkovich, 2020), (III) CIITA protein stability (as shown here), and (IV) HLA-DR degradation and translocation (Hegde and Johnson, 2003; Hegde et al., 2002; Tomazin et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations and data from this study

claims.claim: pUS28 may shield latently infected cells from HLA-II-restricted CD4+ T lymphocytes.
claims.source: Based on the aforementioned role of pUS28 for HCMV latency, it is tempting to speculate that pUS28 may shield latently infected cells from HLA-II-restricted CD4 + T lymphocytes.
claims.evidence: Speculative statement based on the role of pUS28 in latency and its effect on HLA-II

claims.claim: HLA-DR+NKG2C+ memory NK cells are mediators of viral control in transplanted patients.
claims.source: Another intriguing possibility is that a relevant fraction of the HLA-II-mediated CD4 + T cell activation might be elicited by cells that are resistant to HCMV infections, such as the recently described HLA-DR +NKG2C+memory NK cells (Costa-García et al., 2019), which have been shown to be mediators of viral control in transplanted patients (Davis et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Costa-García et al., 2019 and Davis et al., 2015

results.result: IFNγ specifically induces HLA-DP and HLA-DR upregulation on HCMV-permissive fibroblasts in a time-dependent manner, while IFNα and TNFα do not induce HLA-DP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 provide converging evidence from flow cytometry experiments (Figures 1A-C) demonstrating the specificity of IFNγ-induced HLA-II upregulation and its time-dependent nature. The experimental controls with IFNα and TNFα strengthen the conclusion about IFNγ specificity.

results.result: HCMV infection prevents IFNγ-induced HLA-DP upregulation, and this inhibitory effect persists in viral mutants lacking the US2-11 gene region, indicating the existence of unknown viral antagonists outside this region.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 demonstrate through deletion mutant analysis (Figures 1D-E) that HCMV antagonizes HLA-DP induction via factors outside the known US2-11 region. The inference in C21 is logically sound given that deletion of known antagonists did not restore HLA-DP expression.

results.result: pUS28 was identified through screening as an antagonist of CIITA-induced HLA class II expression, significantly and dose-dependently reducing surface expression of HLA-DP, HLA-DR, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DM at various CIITA levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 present a systematic identification and validation of pUS28 function through screening (Figure 2A) followed by dose-response experiments (Figures 2B-F). The data demonstrate reproducible, significant effects across multiple HLA-II molecules with appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: pUS28 reduces CIITA protein levels post-transcriptionally without affecting CIITA mRNA abundance, as demonstrated by unchanged mRNA levels but drastically reduced protein amounts.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 establish the post-transcriptional mechanism through parallel RT-PCR (Figure 3A) and immunoblot (Figure 3B) analyses. The inference in C31 is well-supported by the discordance between mRNA and protein levels, though the specific mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: The CIITA-targeting activity of pUS28 is specific to CIITA and not a general property of viral GPCRs, as control proteins (EYFP) and the related viral GPCR pUS27 do not exhibit this effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 provide appropriate specificity controls using both a non-viral control protein (EYFP) and a closely related viral GPCR (pUS27) shown in Figures 3C-E. These controls effectively rule out non-specific effects and demonstrate pUS28-specific targeting.

results.result: Unbiased mass spectrometry confirmed pUS28-mediated CIITA downregulation and revealed effects on downstream targets including CD74, validating the experimental system and demonstrating that pUS28 affects CIITA target genes independent of their genomic location.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 use orthogonal mass spectrometry validation (Figures 4D-H) that confirms prior findings and extends them to show effects on CD74, a CIITA target outside the MHC-II locus. The inference in C40 is logically sound given CD74's chromosomal location.

results.result: Both gain-of-function (doxycycline-inducible pUS28) and loss-of-function (ΔUS28-HCMV) experiments demonstrate that pUS28 is necessary and sufficient for HLA-II downregulation during HCMV infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 provide complementary genetic evidence through inducible expression (Figure 5A) and viral deletion mutants (Figures 5B-C). The bidirectional genetic approach strengthens the conclusion about pUS28's role, though C43 notes impaired rather than abolished activity, consistent with the redundancy discussed elsewhere.

results.result: The CIITA-targeting function of pUS28 is evolutionarily conserved, as both pUS28 and its MCMV homolog pM33 downregulate human and mouse CIITA.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 demonstrate cross-species conservation through experiments with both human and mouse CIITA (Figures 5D-E). This evolutionary conservation suggests functional importance, though the inference in C45 could benefit from additional functional validation in the MCMV system.

results.result: pUS28 physically interacts with CIITA and reduces its half-life, as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and cycloheximide chase assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 establish direct physical interaction through reciprocal co-IP (Figure 6A) and demonstrate functional consequence through protein stability assays (Figure 6B). The combination of binding and functional data supports a direct mechanism of action.

results.result: A comprehensive panel of degradation pathway inhibitors failed to restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells, suggesting redundant or unusual degradation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 report negative results with multiple inhibitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 4), but the inference in C49 about redundant or unusual mechanisms is speculative. The failure to identify the degradation pathway limits mechanistic understanding, and alternative explanations (e.g., incomplete inhibition, wrong timing, or non-degradative mechanisms) are not fully excluded.

results.result: pUS28 targets CIITA through its C-terminus in a manner independent of G-protein signaling, as the R129A mutant (defective in G-protein coupling) retains activity while C-terminal deletion abolishes CIITA degradation and HLA-II downregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 systematically map functional domains through mutant analysis (Figures 7A-G). The separation of G-protein signaling from CIITA targeting is well-demonstrated, and the requirement for the C-terminus is clearly established through loss-of-function experiments.

results.result: The C-terminus of pUS28 is required for CIITA degradation but not for physical interaction, with amino acids proximal to transmembrane domain 7 being critical for the degradation function.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 dissect the C-terminal function through deletion mapping (Figures 7H-I), demonstrating that binding and degradation are separable functions. The progressive deletion analysis in C60 provides resolution on the critical region, though the specific amino acids remain unidentified.

results.result: pUS28 expression significantly reduces HCMV-specific CD4+ T cell recognition of CIITA-expressing, antigen-loaded cells, demonstrating functional immune evasion through HLA-II-dependent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 demonstrate functional immunological consequences using primary human HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells (Figure 8B). The specificity controls (C62) and the effect of both wild-type and R129A pUS28 (C64) strengthen the conclusion about immune evasion.

results.result: pUS28 inhibits CD4+ T cell production of antiviral cytokines, as supernatants from T cells stimulated in the presence of pUS28 show reduced ability to inhibit HCMV replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 provide functional validation of immune evasion through antiviral activity assays (Figures 8C-D). The reduction in antiviral activity of T cell supernatants provides a biologically relevant readout, though the specific cytokines responsible are not definitively identified.

results.result: HCMV latently infects more than half of adults globally and over 90% of elderly in developing countries, with infection altering more than half of all immune parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish epidemiological and immunological context through citations to peer-reviewed literature (Fowler et al., 2022; Brodin et al., 2015). These are well-established facts in the field that provide appropriate background.

results.result: CD4+ T cells and IFN responses are critical for CMV control, with CD4+ T cell depletion leading to viral reactivation and insufficient CD4+ T cell levels associated with severe clinical outcomes in immunocompromised patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C10 establish the immunological importance of CD4+ T cells through multiple citations to animal models and clinical studies. These provide essential context for the significance of pUS28-mediated immune evasion, though they represent prior work rather than new findings.

results.result: CIITA is the master regulator of HLA-II expression, controlling classical and non-classical HLA-II molecules, with CIITA deficiency causing bare lymphocyte syndrome and susceptibility to severe HCMV infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 establish the biological importance of CIITA through established knowledge and citations. These provide critical context for understanding why pUS28 targeting of CIITA represents an effective immune evasion strategy.

results.result: pUS28 is abundantly expressed during both productive HCMV replication and latency, distinguishing it from most viral proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 establishes the unique expression profile of pUS28 through multiple citations, providing important context for its potential role in immune evasion during different infection stages. This is well-established prior knowledge.

results.result: pUS28 has multiple previously characterized functions including chemokine receptor activity, G-protein signaling, chemokine sequestration, cell migration, potential oncogenic activity, and targeting of innate immune proteins MNDA and IFI16.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C76 summarize prior work on pUS28 functions through appropriate citations. These establish the multifunctional nature of pUS28 and distinguish the CIITA-targeting mechanism (G-protein independent, C76) from other functions. This represents literature review rather than new findings.

results.result: Prior studies have shown that HCMV infection reduces HLA-II expression in latently infected cells and that HCMV employs multiple mechanisms to antagonize HLA-II presentation, including targeting IFN signaling, CIITA transcription, and HLA-DR degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 contextualize the current findings within prior literature, showing that HLA-II antagonism is a known HCMV strategy but that the specific pUS28-CIITA mechanism represents a novel addition to this multipronged attack. These appropriately cite relevant prior work.

results.result: pUS28 may shield latently infected cells from HLA-II-restricted CD4+ T cell recognition.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is explicitly speculative ('tempting to speculate') and represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result. While consistent with the data showing pUS28 expression during latency and its effects on HLA-II, direct evidence for this function during natural latency is not provided.

results.result: HLA-DR+NKG2C+ memory NK cells mediate viral control in transplanted patients and may contribute to HLA-II-mediated immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 cites prior work establishing the role of these NK cells in viral control. This provides context for discussing alternative mechanisms of HLA-II-dependent immunity, though it represents prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: HCMV infection prevents IFNγ-induced upregulation of HLA-DP on fibroblasts. This inhibition occurs even with HCMV mutants lacking the US2-11 gene region, indicating that HCMV encodes unknown antagonists of HLA-DP presentation located outside this region.
results.evaluation: The reviewers describe this as a 'fundamental study' that 'substantially advances our understanding of viral immune evasion by identifying a novel player.' The evidence is characterized as 'compelling, with rigorous immunological assays,' indicating acceptance of these initial findings about HCMV's inhibition of HLA-DP.

results.result: pUS28 was identified through screening as an antagonist of HLA-DP induction and was validated to significantly and dose-dependently diminish CIITA-induced surface expression of multiple HLA class II molecules (HLA-DP, HLA-DR, HLA-DQ) and the peptide editor HLA-DM.
results.evaluation: The reviewers explicitly state the study identifies 'a novel player in this process,' referring to pUS28's role in immune evasion. The characterization of evidence as 'compelling' with 'rigorous immunological assays' supports acceptance of the screening results and validation experiments demonstrating pUS28's broad effects on HLA-II molecules.

results.result: pUS28 exerts a post-transcriptional effect on CIITA, leaving mRNA levels unchanged while drastically reducing CIITA protein amounts.
results.evaluation: The reviewers praise the study for 'uncovering its mode of action' with 'state-of-the-art biochemistry,' which encompasses these mechanistic findings about pUS28's post-transcriptional targeting of CIITA. The compelling evidence statement supports acceptance of this key mechanistic insight.

results.result: The CIITA down-modulating capacity of pUS28 is specific for CIITA and not a general property of viral chemokine receptor homologs, as demonstrated by control experiments with EYFP and the related viral protein pUS27.
results.evaluation: The reviewers' statement about 'rigorous immunological assays' and 'compelling' evidence encompasses these specificity controls, which are standard validation approaches. The acceptance of pUS28 as 'a novel player' implicitly supports the specificity data distinguishing it from pUS27.

results.result: Mass spectrometry and flow cytometry analyses confirmed pUS28's downregulation of CIITA and its target genes including CD74, demonstrating that pUS28 affects CIITA target genes independent of their genomic localization in the MHC-II locus.
results.evaluation: The reviewers specifically highlight 'state-of-the-art biochemistry' as supporting the conclusions, which directly encompasses the mass spectrometry analyses. The characterization of evidence as 'compelling' supports acceptance of these orthogonal validation approaches and the mechanistic insight about genomic localization independence.

results.result: Inducible expression of pUS28 in fibroblasts and infection with ΔUS28-HCMV demonstrated that pUS28 contributes to HCMV's ability to downregulate HLA-II molecules, with the deletion mutant showing impaired HLA-II downregulation compared to wild-type virus.
results.evaluation: The reviewers' statement that the study 'substantially advances our understanding' by identifying pUS28's role encompasses these viral infection experiments. The 'compelling' evidence characterization supports acceptance of both the inducible system and viral deletion mutant data demonstrating pUS28's contribution to viral immune evasion.

results.result: Both pUS28 and its MCMV homolog pM33 downregulate human and mouse CIITA, suggesting the function is evolutionarily conserved across cytomegaloviruses.
results.evaluation: The reviewers note the work will be 'of broad interest to virologists and immunologists,' which is consistent with accepting findings about evolutionary conservation. The 'compelling' evidence statement supports acceptance of the cross-species validation demonstrating conserved function.

results.result: pUS28 and CIITA physically interact and form complexes, with pUS28 reducing the half-life of CIITA as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and cycloheximide chase assays.
results.evaluation: The reviewers explicitly praise the 'state-of-the-art biochemistry' that supports the conclusions, which directly encompasses the co-IP experiments and protein stability assays. These are fundamental biochemical approaches for demonstrating the mechanism of action that reviewers state was successfully 'uncovered.'

results.result: A comprehensive panel of inhibitors targeting various cellular degradation pathways failed to restore CIITA levels in pUS28-expressing cells, suggesting pUS28 reduces CIITA through redundant or unusual degradation processes.
results.evaluation: The reviewers' characterization of 'state-of-the-art biochemistry' and 'compelling' evidence encompasses this systematic investigation of degradation mechanisms. While the negative results don't identify the specific pathway, the reviewers' acceptance of the mode of action being 'uncovered' supports these thorough mechanistic investigations.

results.result: Structure-function analysis revealed that pUS28's effect on CIITA is independent of G-protein signaling (R129A mutant retains activity) but requires the intracellular C terminus, which is indispensable for CIITA degradation and HLA-II downregulation.
results.evaluation: The reviewers state the study 'uncovers its mode of action' with 'compelling' evidence, which directly encompasses these structure-function experiments defining the molecular requirements. The 'rigorous' characterization supports acceptance of the mutational analysis distinguishing signaling-dependent from signaling-independent functions.

results.result: The C-terminal deletion mutant (pUS28-ΔC) still binds CIITA but cannot degrade it, indicating the C terminus affects the degradation machinery rather than the physical interaction. Fine mapping showed amino acids proximal to transmembrane domain 7 are required for CIITA downregulation.
results.evaluation: The reviewers' praise for 'state-of-the-art biochemistry' that 'uncovers the mode of action' encompasses these detailed mechanistic dissections. The 'compelling' evidence statement supports acceptance of the fine structure-function mapping that distinguishes binding from degradation functions.

results.result: HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells from seropositive individuals vigorously responded to CIITA-expressing cells in an HLA-II-dependent manner, but this immune recognition was significantly reduced in the presence of pUS28 or R129A-pUS28.
results.evaluation: The reviewers characterize the evidence as 'compelling, with rigorous immunological assays,' which directly encompasses these functional T cell activation experiments. The statement that the study 'substantially advances our understanding of viral immune evasion' supports acceptance of these data demonstrating the immunological consequences of pUS28 activity.

results.result: Supernatants from HCMV-specific CD4+ T cells stimulated with CIITA-expressing cells showed strong antiviral activity, but this was diminished when cells were stimulated in the presence of pUS28, demonstrating that pUS28 inhibits CD4+ T cell activation and antiviral cytokine production.
results.evaluation: The reviewers' statement about 'rigorous immunological assays' providing 'compelling' evidence encompasses these functional antiviral assays. The characterization of the study as 'substantially advancing understanding of viral immune evasion' supports acceptance of these data linking pUS28's molecular mechanism to functional immune evasion outcomes.

OpenEval R1 focuses specifically on flow cytometry evidence and experimental controls.
